1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3.strategy: The flexible developing move: it guards d4 and e5, prepares castling and keeps every set-up open. It also avoids the pin that 3.Nc3 allows, but it does not prepare e4, so White chooses a quieter, more patient game over a quick pawn centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3.strategy: The traditional move: the knight fights for e4 and d5 and prepares a broad pawn centre. The price is that Black can pin it with the bishop at once, so the game becomes a struggle over the centre rather than a quiet build-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto of the king's bishop, which will press along the long diagonal against Black's queenside while White's king stays safe. White trades the quick e4 advance for lasting pressure, and Black can strike at the centre at once.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Qb3.name: Indian Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Qb3.strategy: Brings the queen out early to eye b7 and d5, but the bishop guards b7, so nothing is threatened. It leaves the d4 pawn without protection, and Black can develop with a gain of time against it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Bg5.name: Indian Defence: Seirawan Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Bg5.background: Also called the Neo-Indian Attack, it is named after the 1980s star Yasser Seirawan. It is rarely played, though the move order was already used by David Janowski against Edward Lasker in New York in 1922.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Bg5.strategy: Pins the knight to the queen to disturb Black's usual development, but the pin is easily broken. Taking on f6 would let Black recapture with the queen, so no pawns are doubled; White gets an unusual set-up without a clear gain.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g4.name: Indian Defence: Devin Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g4.background: Bill Devin played it in 1966 at the Lansing Chess Club, and by 1971 it was known in Michigan as the Devin Gambit. Grandmaster Shakhriyar Mamedyarov played it against Andrey Esipenko at the 2022 Tata Steel Masters.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.g4.strategy: A gambit: the g-pawn is undefended and the knight can take it, but White then builds a big pawn centre with open lines for the pieces. It is a surprise weapon rather than a good plan: White loosens its own king's side, and Black can also decline and simply develop.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4.background: Developed by Aron Nimzowitsch, who introduced it to master-level play in the early twentieth century. Every world champion since Capablanca has played it.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4.strategy: Pins the knight to the king, so White cannot build the centre with e4 for now, and threatens to take on c3 and double White's pawns. Black commits to controlling e4 and to a lasting pawn weakness in return for the bishop pair, and keeps the central pawns flexible.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 d5.strategy: Stakes a claim to the centre with a pawn and gives up the flexibility of the Indian set-ups for a solid, classical structure. The cost is the c8 bishop, which stays shut in behind the e6 pawn until Black finds a way to free it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once, but without the pin White can push d5 and gain space, then build a broad centre. Black gets an unbalanced game with counterplay against that centre, but White holds the space and the easier development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e3.strategy: The flexible main plan: the pawn supports the centre and opens the way for the king's bishop to help control e4. White develops first and does not decide yet how to meet the threat to double the pawns, which leaves a sound, patient game for both sides.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2.strategy: Defends the knight and e4 in one move, so ...Bxc3+ can be met by Qxc3 and White keeps the bishop pair and an undamaged pawn structure. The price is time: the queen has moved early and the kingside pieces wait, so Black looks to open the game quickly and use the lead in development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.g3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Romanishin Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.g3.strategy: Answers the pin with a slow build-up: the king's bishop will fight for the central light squares from a distance instead of White occupying the centre with pawns. White accepts doubled pawns if Black takes on c3, and a quick strike in the centre by Black is the way to meet the plan.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece and keeps every set-up open: White neither provokes the bishop nor commits a pawn, and waits to see how Black means to fight for e4. It also leaves Black to choose between staying in the pin game and a more classical centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Sämisch Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3.background: Named after Fritz Sämisch. Mikhail Botvinnik played it five times against Tal in the 1960 World Championship match, all drawn, and once in the 1961 rematch, a win for White. It is rarely seen nowadays.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3.strategy: Questions the bishop at once: White spends a tempo and accepts doubled c-pawns to get the bishop pair and a broad centre. It is the critical test of Black's plan, since the doubled pawns are either a lasting target or the fuel for a strong pawn centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Leningrad Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5.background: Received its name because its theory was developed extensively by players from Leningrad, such as Boris Spassky.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5.strategy: Matches pin for pin: the bishop ties the f6 knight to the queen, so e4 stays out of reach for both sides and Black's knight no longer guards d5. That makes a space-gaining central pawn advance the natural follow-up, at the cost of leaving the pin on c3 in place.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.f3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Kmoch Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.f3.background: It has no generally accepted name. Florin Gheorghiu played it often early in his career, and Gligorić named it after him; Alexei Shirov used it with great success in the early 1990s before abandoning it after losing three games in a row with it. It is also called the Kmoch Variation.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.f3.strategy: Takes control of e4 with a pawn, so the pinned knight no longer matters and White can build a broad centre. The price is time: the pawn takes the natural square from the g1 knight, and the kingside pieces wait while Black develops.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qd3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Mikenas Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qd3.background: Named after Vladas Mikėnas, and rarely seen.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qd3.strategy: Defends the knight and the e4 square at once, so White can meet ...Bxc3+ with Qxc3 and keep the structure intact. The queen blocks the natural square of the king's bishop and stands exposed in the centre, which is why it stays a rare choice.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Spielmann Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3.background: Named after Rudolf Spielmann, who played it at Carlsbad 1929. It was played at master level in the early 1930s but was soon eclipsed in popularity by 4.Qc2, and it remains uncommon despite occasional revivals by Akopian, Malaniuk and Piket.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3.strategy: Attacks the undefended bishop and defends the knight, so ...Bxc3+ can be met by Qxc3 and White keeps the bishop pair with an intact structure. But from b3 the queen does nothing about e4, and Black can use that square.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e4.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Dilworth Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e4.background: Named after Vernon Dilworth, who contributed an article on the variation to the March 1949 issue of CHESS magazine.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e4.strategy: A gambit that tries to build the full centre at once, but the pinned knight cannot recapture, so Black simply takes the pawn on e4. The pressure White gets in return does not make up for it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+.strategy: Cashes in the pin at once: the bishop is given up for the knight so that White's pawns are doubled on the c-file, a lasting weakness. Retreating instead would waste the move, because White would then build the centre with e4 for free.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Be7.strategy: Retreats the bishop and so gives up the whole point of the pin: with the pin gone, White plays e4 for free and builds a big centre. Black has conceded space without getting the doubled pawns.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Ba5.strategy: Keeps the pin but loses the bishop: b4 chases it to b6 and c5 traps it, so Black can only give it up for a pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5..strategy: Recaptures with the pawn, the only way to do it. White accepts doubled pawns and a weak pawn on c4 in return for the bishop pair, a broad centre and the chance of a quick attack on the kingside.
Blocks the check without taking the bishop, and loses a piece: Black captures on d2 with check, and after the recapture has won a whole knight.
Interposes the queen, which ...Bxd2+ simply takes: White has lost a knight and a queen for a bishop.

Blockades the doubled pawns and hits d4 at once. Black's plan is to pile up on the weak c4 pawn while White builds the centre, so the game turns on whether White's centre and kingside play outweigh that target.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5..name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Sämisch Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5..strategy: Gets the king to safety before the centre opens and keeps the plans against the doubled pawns in reserve. The cost is that White can start building the pawn centre without hindrance, so Black must still find a way to fight it.

Prepares to attack the weak pawn on c4 with the bishop on a6, which White can defend only awkwardly. Black delays the blockade pawn, so White may build the centre at once and Black must then act quickly against it.

Develops a piece towards a5, where it eyes the c4 pawn, and adds pressure on d4. Black keeps both a central strike and a blockade of the doubled pawns available, but White can start building a broad centre, so the counterplay has to come quickly.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5..name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Sämisch Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5..strategy: Adds a defender to d4 and opens the way for the king's bishop, which also guards c4. White answers the pressure with a solid chain and keeps the central advance in hand, so the weak pawns are shielded while the pieces come out.

Supports an e4 push that the knight on f6 cannot disturb and aims at a broad pawn centre. The price is that the pawn takes the natural square of the kingside knight and loosens the king, so that knight usually comes out via e2.
Develops naturally and guards d4 and e5, but does not prepare e4, which the knight on f6 holds under control. White stays flexible, yet Black gets time to attack the c4 pawn and the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5..name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Sämisch Variation, O'Kelly Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.a3 Bxc3+ 5..strategy: Prepares ...Ba6 against the weak c4 pawn, so White has to defend it or give it up. Black plays against the doubled pawns on the queenside, and the pawn on b6 also gives the c8 bishop its diagonal.

Develops with threats: the knight adds to the pressure on d4 and can go to a5 to attack the weak pawn on c4. Black keeps every plan against the doubled pawns available while White still has to finish development, which makes it the most flexible move.

Gets the king out of the centre before White's pieces reach their posts. The plans against c4 are only delayed, but White meanwhile builds the centre freely and may play for a kingside attack, so Black must be ready to react quickly.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5 h6.strategy: Puts the question to the bishop at once and makes room for the king. If White gives up the bishop for the knight and Black recaptures with the queen, Black gets two bishops against bishop and knight, so White has to keep the tension.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5 c5.strategy: Challenges d4 at once and lets White commit to the d5 advance before Black decides how to answer the pin. It leads to the same kind of unbalanced game, with White's space set against the dark-square play of Black's pieces.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece against d4 and prepares to claim the centre with a pawn, ignoring the bishop for the moment. The pin on f6 remains, so White can gain space or trade on f6, and Black's king stays in the centre a little longer.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5 h6 5.Bh.strategy: Declines the trade and keeps the pin on the f6 knight, so Black's knight still cannot freely move or guard d5. The price is a bishop placed far from the queenside, where Black may later harass it with a kingside pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5 h6 5.Bx.strategy: Gives up the bishop for the knight at once, so Black recaptures with the queen and keeps the two bishops. White loses the pin, which was the point of Bg5; the trade is playable but hands Black the long-term trump.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5 h6 5.Bd.strategy: Retreats and gives up the pin: White has spent two moves for the bishop to return to d2, where it guards c3 and takes the sting out of ...Bxc3. A safe route to a quiet game, but Black has gained the useful ...h6 for free.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5 h6 5.Bh.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once. It forces White to decide whether to release the tension or to gain space, and it keeps both a pawn exchange and a closed blockade of the dark squares available to Black.

Challenges the bishop directly: it must retreat to g3, where ...Ne4 can trade it off, and the pinned knight on c3 cannot take the intruder. Black frees the f6 knight and gains space, but the advance weakens the kingside and keeps the king from castling there safely.

Doubles White's pawns at once, but gives up the bishop pair while the knight on f6 is still pinned to the queen. White gets the bishops and a free hand in the centre in return for a damaged queenside, so Black must break the pin soon.

The point of the pin: with the f6 knight tied down, White grabs space and attacks e6 right away. Black must decide whether to open the position against the new pawn or to close it and fight for the dark squares.

Keeps the centre intact and develops the king's bishop; the pin stays. White does not gain space with d5, so Black can release the tension by exchanging on d4 and the game becomes a quiet, manoeuvring one.
Takes the pawn, but cannot keep it: Black retakes on c5 at once with the bishop. White has traded the d4 pawn that held the centre for Black's c-pawn and gained nothing from it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5 h6 5.Bh.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Leningrad Variation, Benoni Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5 h6 5.Bh.strategy: Supports a pawn on e5 and keeps the e6 pawn's options open: Black can capture on d5 or, more usually, give up the bishop on c3 and blockade the dark squares. The position then favours Black's knights over White's bishops.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5 h6 5.Bh.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Leningrad Variation, Averbakh Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5 h6 5.Bh.background: Much played in the 1970s, after Mikhail Tal scored a crushing win over Boris Spassky at Tallinn 1973.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Bg5 h6 5.Bh.strategy: A pawn sacrifice that attacks the undefended c4 pawn, the support of White's d5 pawn, from the flank. The knight on c3 is pinned and cannot take it, but Black has to prove that open lines against the centre are worth the pawn.

Trades the bishop for the knight to double White's pawns before the centre closes. Black gives up the bishop pair, but the doubled pawns and the pinned f6 knight leave White with problems to solve, and Black can then blockade the dark squares with pawns.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.f3 d5.strategy: Takes e4 out of White's reach: the d-pawn and the f6 knight both control it, so f3 has bought nothing for the centre. The pawn move has weakened White's kingside and delayed development, while Black fights for the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.f3 c5.strategy: Strikes at White's centre from the flank. If White pushes the d-pawn, White has more space and Black plays against it with queenside pawn breaks; the f3 pawn has weakened White's kingside and cost development time, so the space comes at a price.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.f3 Nc6.strategy: Develops and adds pressure on d4, but does little to stop White building the broad centre that f3 prepared. Black has to fight it later with piece play and pawn breaks, so the move is sound but hands White the plan the f3 pawn was played for.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.f3 d5 5.a3.strategy: Puts the question to the bishop. If Black takes on c3, White gets the bishop pair and doubled c-pawns, and with the f-pawn on f3 the e4 advance can follow with a broad centre. Retreating lets White build the centre in peace.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.f3 d5 5.cxd.strategy: Settles the central tension at once. After ...exd5 White's d4 pawn is firm, but Black's pawn on d5 keeps e4 under control, so the broad centre that f3 was meant to build is out of reach for now. A solid, slow game in which White must find a use for the f3 pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.f3 d5 5.Bg5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and pins the f6 knight to the queen. Black can ask the bishop what it wants and the pin is easily broken, so the move gains little, and the f3 pawn still does nothing for White's development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.f3 d5 5.a3.strategy: Takes the knight and doubles White's pawns, giving up the bishop pair. White's f3 does nothing for development, so Black has time to attack the doubled pawns.

Declines to double White's pawns and keeps both of Black's bishops. The pin ends, so White is free to build the broad pawn centre, and Black has to counter it with timely pawn breaks; the f3 and a3 moves have cost White development, which keeps the game balanced.
Declines the exchange but invites c4-c5, which hits the bishop with tempo and gains space. After the retreat White has a free hand to set up the broad centre that f3 was meant for.

The only sound recapture: blocking the check or moving the king leaves White a piece down. White gets the bishop pair and a pawn mass on c3, c4 and d4 with an advance of the e-pawn in mind; the doubled pawns and the loosened kingside are the price.
Blocks the check instead of retaking, so the knight is never won back: after ...Bxd2+ the bishops come off and White is a whole piece down.
Steps out of the check without retaking, so Black has simply won a knight for nothing. White has also given up castling, and the king on f2 is exposed to further checks.
Attacks d4 at once, and with the d-pawn already hitting c4, both the c4 and d4 pawns come under pressure. White has to open the centre quickly, since only open lines give the bishops their scope.

Gets the king to safety before White's centre rolls forward. Black keeps the pawns on d5 and e6 and the pressure on c4, and plays to blockade the doubled pawns, with White's bishops as the long-term worry.

Develops and adds pressure on d4, but it leaves the king in the centre and does nothing about the c4 pawn, so White can open the centre on its own terms. Playable, but White gets the broad centre it wants.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3 c5.strategy: The natural counter: the queen attacks the bishop on b4 but does not guard e4, and the pawn both defends the bishop and strikes at d4. Black exploits the poor placement of the queen, and White must decide how to deal with the tension.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3 Nc6.strategy: Defends the attacked bishop by developing a piece and presses on d4. The queen on b3 does not watch e4, so Black can still bring the other knight there, and White has no clear way to exploit the early queen sortie.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3 Bxc3+.strategy: Takes the knight so that the queen has to recapture and White never gets doubled pawns. Black gives White the two bishops without a structural weakness, and the queen on c3 is hit by ...Ne4, so White loses a little time; sound but slightly passive.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3 c5 5.dx.strategy: Takes the pawn and removes the one that defended the bishop, so the queen attacks it at once. The extra pawn is exposed, and Black's quick development and the e4 square mean White may have to give it back, but this is the principal test of the early queen.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3 c5 5.a3.strategy: Puts the question to the bishop at once. If it takes on c3, the queen recaptures and White has the two bishops with an undamaged pawn structure; if it retreats, White has gained time and space and the pin is gone.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3 c5 5.Nf.strategy: Develops the knight and keeps the pawn on d4 guarded instead of taking on c5. White leaves the central tension to Black; the queen on b3 stays awkward, since it does not guard e4, and Black has no difficulty equalising.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3 c5 5.dx.name: Nimzo-Indian Defence: Spielmann Variation, Romanovsky Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qb3 c5 5.dx.strategy: Defends the bishop and develops, with the pawn on c5 already under fire from the bishop. Black offers the pawn for speed: the knight on f6 can then go to e4, where White's queen does not reach.

Takes the pawn back at once with the bishop, so material is level and Black develops compactly. The bishop leaves the pin on c3, though: White's knight is free again and can harass the bishop, which gives White time to develop.

Steps back along the diagonal, keeping the pin, so the knight on c3 still cannot move. White is a pawn up for the moment, but the pawn on c5 is weak, and Black plays to recover it; the cost is time spent on the bishop.

The main line: White develops and keeps the extra pawn, accepting that the queen on b3 does not control e4. Black's knight lands there at once, pressing the pinned knight and the c5 pawn, so White has to defend carefully while Black leads in development.

Unpins the knight at once, so a capture on c3 can be answered with the bishop and not the queen. It does nothing for the c5 pawn or the e4 square, though, and Black regains the pawn at will with an easy game.

Solid, and it opens the king's bishop, but it leaves e4 to Black, whose knight lands there at once and attacks the pinned knight and the c5 pawn. White develops slowly while the extra pawn is under fire.

The point of the line: the queen on b3 does not control e4, so the knight arrives with effect. It joins the bishop in piling up on the pinned knight on c3 and attacks the c5 pawn, which Black regains with a lead in development.

Regains the pawn at once and keeps both bishops, but it releases the pin and the pressure on c3, so White finishes developing in peace. Black has a sound game, though it gives up the early initiative.
Takes the knight, and the queen recaptures on c3 and eyes g7: ...Ne4 then hangs that pawn, and Black has no easy way to win back the pawn on c5. White keeps the bishop pair and the extra pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 c5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and adds a defender to d4, which the c-pawn attacks. White leaves the centre tension unresolved and keeps a flexible game in which neither side has fixed its pawn structure yet, and the recapture on d4 would be made with a piece.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 c5 4.d5.strategy: The principled answer: it grabs space and creates an unbalanced structure. After the exchange on d5 White holds the centre and the extra space, while Black has a queenside pawn majority and a half-open e-file. White aims at a central break, Black at counterplay against the d5 pawn and on the queenside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 c5 4.e3.strategy: Solid and flexible: it supports d4 and opens the bishop, but it leaves Black the choice. Black can exchange on d4 and equalise with an early pawn push to d5, which gives a quiet, nearly symmetrical structure and little for White to play for.
